title: Understanding Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
summary: PCOS is a common endocrine and metabolic condition characterized by hormonal imbalances that can affect ovulation, cycle regularity, and androgen levels.
keyPoints: PCOS is an endocrine (hormonal) condition, not an infectious disease or cancer.

Doctors assess it using established international criteria (such as the Rotterdam criteria), which require at least two of: irregular ovulation/periods, higher androgen signs (like excess facial hair or acne), or multiple small ovarian follicles on ultrasound.
Having follicles on the ovaries does not automatically mean PCOS; similarly, one can have PCOS without visible ovarian cysts.
It is a manageable condition that clinicians and individuals navigate with tailored lifestyle, nutritional, and clinical care.
source: Monash University / International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (2023)

title: Frequent Signs Observed Across Cycles
summary: PCOS presents differently in every body. Symptoms often relate to reproductive hormones, metabolic sensitivity, and skin health.
keyPoints: Irregular, delayed, or infrequent menstrual periods (cycles longer than 35 days or fewer than 8 cycles per year).
Persistent or adult-onset acne, particularly along the jawline and chin.
Increased hair growth on the face, chest, abdomen, or upper thighs (hirsutism).
Scalp hair thinning or excessive hair shedding (androgenic alopecia).
Difficulty losing weight or unexplained weight gain related to insulin resistance.
Pelvic discomfort, bloating, or fatigue across menstrual phases.
source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) Practice Bulletin No. 194

title: Why Similar Symptoms Can Have Several Origins
summary: The endocrine system is interconnected. Symptoms overlapping with PCOS are frequently caused by other distinct and treatable conditions.
keyPoints: Thyroid disorders (Hypothyroidism or Hyperthyroidism) can alter menstrual frequency, skin hydration, hair loss, and body weight.
Hyperprolactinemia (elevated prolactin hormone) can pause or delay regular ovulation.
Hypothalamic amenorrhea caused by high psychological stress, overtraining, or rapid caloric restriction can halt periods.
Endometriosis or adenomyosis can cause severe pelvic pain and heavy or painful bleeding.
Nutritional deficiencies (such as severe Vitamin D or Iron deficiency) can cause fatigue, cycle delays, and hair thinning.
source: The Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on PCOS and Ovulatory Disorders

title: Knowing When to Schedule a Routine Visit vs Seek Urgent Attention
summary: Understanding when to book a doctor consultation helps you advocate for your health safely.
keyPoints: Schedule a routine consultation if your periods come less frequently than every 35 days, or if you miss periods for 3 consecutive months.
Consult a doctor if you experience progressive facial hair, worsening cystic acne, or unexplained weight shifts.

Seek urgent or emergency care immediately if you experience severe sudden pelvic pain, very heavy bleeding (soaking through more than one pad per hour for two consecutive hours), or fainting/dizziness with bleeding.
source: National Health Service (NHS) Clinical Guidance on Menstrual Health and Emergency Gynecological Evaluation

title: How to Prepare for Your Gynecologist Appointment
summary: Bringing a structured symptom timeline and specific questions empowers you to have a productive, collaborative discussion.
keyPoints: Track cycle dates: Note your last 3–6 period start dates and duration.
Record symptom frequency and severity: Note when acne, facial hair, or cramps appear.
Bring medication history: Note any supplements, birth control, or thyroid medications you have taken.
Prepare key questions: Ask which blood tests (FSH, LH, Total/Free Testosterone, TSH, Prolactin, Fasting Insulin) or pelvic imaging are recommended.
Remember: You have the right to ask for clarification, a respectful environment, and a differential evaluation.
source: World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines on Patient Empowerment and Reproductive Health Navigation
